content: 1. Diagnostic tests for kala-azar (KA), post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL), and other related conditions are utilized at various levels of healthcare facilities to ensure accurate detection and management of these diseases. 2. First-line and second-line treatment protocols for KA and PKDL are implemented at different tiers of healthcare facilities, tailored to the severity of the disease and the resources available at each level. 3. A robust quality control system is in place to ensure the reliability and accuracy of diagnostic procedures for KA and PKDL. 4. Comprehensive training and capacity-building initiatives are conducted to enhance the skills of healthcare professionals involved in the diagnosis, treatment, and management of KA and PKDL. 5. Integrated vector management strategies are employed in endemic areas, including the use of guidelines for indoor residual spraying (IRS) with insecticides, monitoring the quality of spraying, and implementing quality assurance mechanisms. 6. Insecticide-treated nets and environmental management practices are incorporated into the program to reduce vector populations and minimize disease transmission. 7. Entomological surveillance is conducted both before and after spraying activities to monitor vector populations and assess insecticide resistance. 8. Monitoring and quality control processes are established to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions and ensure the accuracy of data collected. 9. Internal and external monitoring committees are formed to oversee activities and provide recommendations for improvement. 10. Cross-border collaboration is facilitated among implementation units, districts, states, and countries to address the transnational nature of disease transmission and ensure coordinated efforts. 11. The process of validating the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem in South-East Asia involves meeting specific criteria and documenting achievements formally. 12. Operational research is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions, identify gaps, and generate evidence for improving control and elimination strategies. 13. Publications related to the control and elimination of KA in endemic countries are compiled to disseminate knowledge and share best practices. 14. Annual reports are generated to document the number of endemic units, populations at risk, incidence rates of KA and PKDL, and the outcomes of active case-finding efforts. 15. The proportion of private health facilities reporting KA cases and the adequacy of diagnostic facilities in healthcare settings are monitored to ensure comprehensive coverage. 16. Operational research is undertaken to estimate the proportion of unreported cases and address gaps in surveillance systems. 17. Updated national strategic guidelines for the elimination of kala-azar are developed and included in the dossier, along with standard operating procedures (SOPs) for key activities. 18. Innovative information, education, and communication (IEC) and behavior change communication (BCC) strategies are tailored to the specific needs of individual states. 19. A comprehensive monitoring and evaluation (M&E) strategy is implemented to assess progress and guide future actions. 20. Definitions of control, elimination, and eradication of neglected tropical diseases are established, considering the diversity of pathogens, epidemiology, and transmission dynamics. 21. Control refers to reducing disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and/or mortality to locally acceptable levels through deliberate efforts, with continued interventions required to maintain the reduction. 22. Elimination of transmission involves reducing the incidence of infection caused by a specific pathogen to zero in a defined geographical area, with minimal risk of reintroduction. 23. Elimination as a public health problem is defined by achieving measurable global targets set by WHO, requiring continued actions to sustain the targets and prevent re-establishment of transmission. 24. Eradication refers to the permanent reduction to zero of a specific pathogen, with no risk of reintroduction, achieved through deliberate efforts. 25. Extinction occurs when a specific pathogen no longer exists in nature or laboratories, which may happen with or without deliberate efforts. 26. The certification process for eradication involves an international commission verifying and granting certification to countries while maintaining surveillance until all countries are certified. 27. Validation of elimination as a public health problem or verification of transmission elimination is assessed against objective criteria and formally recorded. 28. The WHO roadmap on neglected tropical diseases sets targets for the eradication and elimination of specific diseases at global, regional, or country levels. 29. Standard operating procedures for validating elimination as a public health problem or verifying transmission elimination are established and standardized. 30. Member States are responsible for preparing dossiers for validation, verification, or certification, with technical assistance provided by WHO if requested. 31. WHO headquarters maintains a repository of dossiers, ensuring systematic review and removal of duplicate information. 32. The Reviewing Authority evaluates dossiers and decides on validation, verification, or certification within one year of receipt. 33. Feedback on dossiers is provided by WHO, summarizing the Reviewing Authority's comments and decisions. 34. If the claim of elimination is accepted, the summary is forwarded to the WHO Director-General for official acknowledgment. 35. Post-validation, verification, or certification activities include continued surveillance and commitment to sustaining the disease burden under targeted thresholds. 36. WHO acknowledges achievements in annual disease-specific articles published in the Weekly Epidemiological Record and updates the endemicity status of Member States in the Global Health Observatory.
